opus-5.5.text:
It really grew out of frustration, honestly. Before TVM, I'd spent a lot of time on XGBoost and then on MXNet, and through that work I kept running into the same wall. Every time a new model architecture came out, or a new piece of hardware showed up, someone had to sit down and hand-write optimized kernels for it. That worked when there were one or two dominant GPUs and a handful of standard operators, but you could already see the landscape fragmenting: mobile phones, different GPU vendors, FPGAs, and then all these specialized accelerators people were starting to design.

So the question in my head was: is this sustainable? If every combination of model and hardware needs a team of experts writing low-level code by hand, the whole field gets bottlenecked on a very small number of people. And the most interesting new hardware ideas would struggle to get adopted, because nobody would have the software stack to run real models on them.

Compilers were the natural answer to that kind of problem. Historically, that's exactly what compilers did for general-purpose programming: you write at a higher level, and the compiler maps it efficiently onto the machine. But traditional compilers weren't really designed for deep learning workloads. The structure is different: big tensor operations, lots of freedom in how you tile and fuse and lay out memory, and a search space of possible implementations that's enormous.

What made me excited was realizing we could combine two things I cared about. One was the systems and compiler side, with ideas like separating the description of the computation from the schedule of how it runs, which Halide had shown was powerful. The other was machine learning itself. Instead of relying purely on handcrafted heuristics, we could use learning to explore that huge space of implementations and find good ones automatically. That's where things like AutoTVM came from.

There was also a community dimension. I saw that the way to make this real wasn't just to write a paper, but to build an open-source stack that people could actually use and extend for their own hardware. Working in the open with people from industry and academia ended up shaping TVM as much as any single technical idea did.

So it wasn't one moment of revelation. It was more that, from my previous projects, I kept seeing the gap between where models were going and where hardware was going, and machine-learning compilation felt like the bridge that needed to be built.

r001.rationale: The response describes reducing reliance on scarce kernel experts, but does not identify enabling small teams to build machine-learning systems quickly as a goal.

r002.rationale: It says the bottleneck persisted through earlier work on XGBoost and MXNet, but does not mention CXXNet.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. It really came out of pain, honestly. Around the time I was working on XGBoost and then MXNet, I kept running into the same wall: you'd design a nice model, and then the real work was getting it to actually run fast on whatever hardware you had. If you were on an NVIDIA GPU with cuDNN, great. But the moment you wanted to run on a phone, or a new accelerator, or even just an operator that the vendor library didn't cover, you were back to hand-writing kernels. And every framework was doing this separately, duplicating the same effort.

What struck me was that this looked a lot like the problem compilers had already solved for general-purpose programs. We don't hand-write assembly for every CPU anymore. So the question became: why are we doing that for deep learning? The models have very regular structure, lots of dense tensor operations, so in some ways they're a better target for compilation than arbitrary C code.

The other piece that made it click was the Halide idea of separating what you compute from how you schedule it. Once you have that separation, you can keep the algorithm fixed and search over the schedule, and that opened the door to using machine learning itself to find good kernels, which became AutoTVM and later the auto-scheduling work. That was the moment it felt like a real research direction rather than just engineering cleanup: machine learning for compiling machine learning.

And then the broader motivation was about who gets to participate. If only a handful of companies with big kernel teams can make models run well on their hardware, the ecosystem gets very narrow. A compiler stack that's open and retargetable lets a small team bring up a new chip, or lets a researcher deploy to the edge without a vendor's blessing. That's what kept me on it even when it was a lot of unglamorous infrastructure work.

r001.rationale: The response says a small team could bring up a new chip, but does not identify quickly building machine-learning systems as the motivating goal.

r002.rationale: It describes a persistent performance bottleneck during work on XGBoost and MXNet, but does not mention CXXNet as the criterion requires.

astra-6.text:
For me, it came from thinking about the gap between developing a machine-learning model and actually running it efficiently. You can describe a computation at a fairly high level, but getting good performance on a particular device often requires a lot of specialized work. And as models and hardware change, you have to keep doing that work again.

I started to see this as a compilation problem: could we build a system that takes the computation people want to express and helps translate it into an efficient implementation across different hardware? That became the motivation for TVM. The interesting challenge was how much of that optimization process we could automate, so that deploying a new model wouldn’t always depend on someone hand-tuning every operation.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on automating efficient deployment across hardware; it does not identify enabling small teams to build machine-learning systems quickly as a motivating goal.

r002.rationale: It does not mention CXXNet, MXNet, or a bottleneck that persisted despite those earlier efforts.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it came from thinking about the gap between developing a machine-learning model and actually making it run efficiently. You can describe the computation at a fairly high level, but getting good performance on a particular device often requires a lot of specialized work. And when the model or the hardware changes, you have to do that work again.

That felt like a compiler problem. Could we take a high-level description of a model and systematically transform it into an efficient implementation for different hardware? Instead of hand-tuning every operator for every device, could we build a system that helps automate that process?

That was the direction behind TVM: making it easier to bring models to different hardware while still getting good performance.

r001.rationale: The response describes automating efficient model deployment across hardware, but does not identify enabling small teams to build machine-learning systems quickly as a motivating goal.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention CXXNet or MXNet, or say that a bottleneck persisted despite Tianqi Chen’s earlier efforts.
